chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

A man left Medina intending for Iraq, so two black men followed him, one of them being a slave of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). When he reached Al-Aws, the man slept, so they took a rock and cracked his head with it. They were seized and brought to Muhammad ibn Khalid, and the guardians of the slain man came and asked him to execute retaliation upon them, but he disliked doing so. He asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about that, but he did not answer him.

Abd al-Rahman said: 'I thought he disliked answering him because he did not view that two should be killed for one.' So the guardians of the slain man complained of Muhammad ibn Khalid and his action to the people of Medina. The people of Medina said to them: 'If you want him to execute retaliation upon you, then follow Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) and complain to him of your grievances.'

So they did so, and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Execute retaliation upon them.' When they called them to execute retaliation, the face of the slave of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) turned black until it became like ink. This was mentioned to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), so they said: 'May Allah keep you well! When he was brought forward to be killed, his face turned black until it became like ink.' He said: 'He was disbelieving in Allah openly.' So both were killed.

key_terms.جَعْفَرَ بْنَ مُحَمَّدٍ: Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on Qisas when one of the killers is a slave and displays signs of open disbelief?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the Shia juristic principle that the status of 'free' versus 'slave' in Qisas (retaliation) is determined by the individual's actual condition at the time of the crime, not merely their master's status. The Imam’s hesitation and subsequent confirmation highlight the nuance that while two free lives are required for one, a slave's execution does not necessarily require a second free life unless specific conditions like open disbelief (kufr) or master's consent apply. The narrative serves as a practical demonstration of how hidden attributes, such as the slave's public apostasy, can influence judicial rulings in the Imams' era.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Safwan Bin Yahya, from Abdul Rahman Bin Al Hajjaj who said,

‘A man went out from Al-Medina intending for Al-Iraq. So two black men followed him, one of them being a slave of Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>. So when he came to Al-Aws, the man slept. So they both took a rock and cracked his head with it. So they were both seized, and Muhammad Bin Khalid came with them both, and the guardians of the killed-one came over and asked him for the retaliation, but he did not like that to be done. So Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> was asked about that, but he<sup>asws</sup> did not answer him.

Abdul Rahman said, ‘So I guessed that he<sup>asws</sup> did not like answering him because he<sup>asws</sup> did not view that two should be killed for one. So the guardians of the killed-one complained of Muhammad Bin Khalid and his dealings, to the people of Al-Medina. So the people of Al-Medina said to him, ‘If you intend the retaliation from him, so follow Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> Bin Muhammad<sup>asws</sup>. So complain to him<sup>asws</sup> of your grievances.

So they did it. So Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> said: 'Retaliate them’. So when they called them over for their retaliation, the face of the slave of Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> turned black until it became as if it was the ink. So that was mentioned to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, so they said, ‘May Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Keep you<sup>asws</sup> well! When he was brought forward to be killed, his face blackened until it became as if it was the ink’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘He had disbelieved in Allah<sup>azwj</sup> openly’. So both of them were killed’.
